title: Mosaic colourwork scarf
subtitle: A two-colour slip-stitch scarf with no floats.
excerpt: A scarf knitted flat in mosaic colourwork on 4 mm needles with DK-weight yarn, finishing at 18 cm wide by 155 cm long. Mosaic knitting alternates two-row stripes of each colour, slipping stitches from the previous colour instead of stranding, so only one yarn is worked at a time and there are no floats on the wrong side.
sourceNotes: Mosaic knitting as a non-stranded colourwork technique was popularised by Barbara Walker in A Treasury of Knitting Patterns (1968) and Mosaic Knitting (1976). Slip-stitch colour patterns have older precedents in Victorian knitting manuals. This chart is original.
heroPrompt: A finished mosaic colourwork scarf in charcoal and mustard DK yarn, photographed folded to show the geometric slip-stitch pattern, with the clean wrong side visible at the fold.

glossaryTerms.definition: A non-stranded colourwork technique in which two yarn colours alternate in pairs of rows. On each pair of rows, stitches in the contrast colour are slipped rather than worked, creating a coloured pattern without any floats on the wrong side.

content.text: This is a scarf knitted flat in
mosaic colourwork

on 4 mm needles with DK-weight yarn, finishing at 18 cm wide and 155 cm long when blocked. In mosaic knitting two colours alternate in pairs of rows. On each pair of rows only one colour is worked; the other colour's stitches are
slipped purlwise
to carry the colour upward without stranding across the row. The wrong side has short vertical floats of one stitch each rather than long horizontal ones.

Mosaic colourwork is classified INTERMEDIATE rather than ADVANCED because there are no floats to manage and only one yarn is in the hand at any time. The main skill is reading the chart and tracking which colour is active on each pair of rows. The finished scarf needs about 220 m (approximately 80 g) each of DK-weight colour A and colour B.
What you need

items.name: DK-weight yarn, colour A
items.substitutions: Any DK-weight smooth yarn. High contrast between A and B gives the clearest pattern.

items.name: 4 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 8 / US 6)

content.text: Gauge

22 sts x 30 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked. Mosaic colourwork typically rows at approximately 34 rows per 10 cm (fewer rows per cm than plain stocking stitch) because the slip stitches elongate. Swatch the chart pattern and measure after blocking. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by approximately 0.9 cm.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

in colour A to place 40 stitches on the needle. The stitch count is a multiple of 8 for the chart repeat. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 4 mm needles (circumference approximately 12.6 mm) and 40 stitches: (12.6 x 40) / 10 + 15 = 50.4 + 15 = about 65 cm. Leave at least 65 cm of tail in colour A.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 40 stitches on the needle.
Body
Join colour B at the right edge on a RS row. The two yarns sit at the right edge and alternate as follows:

Rows 1–2 (colour A): RS: work A stitches in K, slip V stitches purlwise with yarn at back. WS: work A stitches in P, slip V stitches purlwise with yarn at front. After row 2, slide colour A to the right edge without cutting.
Rows 3–4 (colour B): RS: work A stitches in K (with B), slip V stitches. WS: work A stitches in P (with B), slip V stitches. After row 4, slide colour B to the right edge.
Repeat [rows 1–4] across the full length. Continue until the scarf measures 155 cm from the cast-on edge.
Stitch count check-in: at the halfway mark (approximately row 265) you should have 40 stitches on the needle.
Bind off
Work a standard bind-off in the current active colour on a RS row. The bind-off edge should match the cast-on edge elasticity.
Common faults

Pattern scrambled or misaligned. The V positions in the chart shift the slip stitches upward by one colour cycle. If you accidentally work a V stitch instead of slipping it, the pattern breaks at that point. For long mosaic patterns, mark the active row on the chart with a sticky note and move it only at the end of each two-row pair.

Yarn tangling at the right edge. Because neither yarn is cut between uses, both hang at the right edge. Keep them on separate small bobbins or balls, and untwist when you turn the work between every two-row pair.

Slipped stitches pulling fabric in at the sides. The slip stitches across the full row collect the fabric toward them. If the width narrows at the sides, ensure you spread the slipped stitches on the right needle before slipping so the float behind them is generous rather than tight.
Finishing
Weave in all tails. Block by soaking in cool water, pressing out water, and pinning to 18 x 155 cm. The mosaic pattern evens out and the stitch definition improves significantly after blocking.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat to dry. Reblock if the slip stitches contract after washing.
What to try next

The Fair Isle scarf uses full stranding instead of slipping, giving a different graphic effect and a warmer, denser fabric. The slip-stitch checkers scarf is a simpler slip-stitch colourwork pattern using a 4-row repeat that is beginner-friendly.
